sections.title: 3. Methodology
sections.text: 3. Methodology We propose ReinPool , a framework that learns to dynamically filter and pool multi-vector embeddings. In this section, we first formulate the document representation problem, then introduce the ReinPool agent, and finally describe the training strategy based on inverse retrieval. 3.1. Problem Formulation Let a document [LaTeX: d] d d be projected into a sequence of [LaTeX: N] N N embedding vectors [LaTeX: V_{d}=\{v_{1},v_{2},\dots,v_{N}\}] V d = { v 1 , v 2 , … , v N } V_{d}=\{v_{1},v_{2},\dots,v_{N}\} , where [LaTeX: v_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{model}}] v i ∈ ℝ d m ​ o ​ d ​ e ​ l v_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{model}} . While storing [LaTeX: V_{d}] V d V_{d} fully preserves fine-grained details, it incurs high storage and retrieval costs. Our goal is to learn a mapping [LaTeX: f:\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{model}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d_{model}}] f : ℝ N × d m ​ o ​ d ​ e ​ l → ℝ d m ​ o ​ d ​ e ​ l f:\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{model}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d_{model}} that compresses the multi-vector sequence into a single vector [LaTeX: \mathbf{v}_{\text{pool}}] 𝐯 pool \mathbf{v}_{\text{pool}} , while maximizing retrieval performance. ReinPool achieves this by selectively filtering vectors via a reinforcement learning policy before aggregating the retained set. 3.2. ReinPool Framework The ReinPool process consists of two stages: Filtering and Pooling . 3.2.1. Filtering Policy We employ a policy network [LaTeX: \pi_{\theta}] π θ \pi_{\theta} to identify a subset of informative vectors. For each vector [LaTeX: v_{t}\in V_{d}] v t ∈ V d v_{t}\in V_{d} , the agent outputs a binary action [LaTeX: a_{t}\in\{0,1\}] a t ∈ { 0 , 1 } a_{t}\in\{0,1\} : • If [LaTeX: a_{t}=1] a t = 1 a_{t}=1 : Keep vector [LaTeX: v_{t}] v t v_{t} . • If [LaTeX: a_{t}=0] a t = 0 a_{t}=0 : Discard vector [LaTeX: v_{t}] v t v_{t} . The set of retained vectors is denoted as [LaTeX: V_{\text{keep}}=\{v_{t}\mid a_{t}=1\}] V keep = { v t ∣ a t = 1 } V_{\text{keep}}=\{v_{t}\mid a_{t}=1\} . The policy model [LaTeX: \pi_{\theta}] π θ \pi_{\theta} is implemented as a Transformer-based architecture ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) comprising a multi-head attention layer (8 heads) followed by a linear classification head. Crucially, the number of parameters in [LaTeX: \pi_{\theta}] π θ \pi_{\theta} is [LaTeX: O(d_{model}^{2})] O ⁡ ( d m ​ o ​ d ​ e ​ l 2 ) O(d_{model}^{2}) , which is negligible compared to the underlying embedding model. The objective of [LaTeX: \pi_{\theta}] π θ \pi_{\theta} is not to transform the embedding space, but rather to eliminate redundant or non-informative vectors. 3.2.2. Pooling The filtered subset of vectors is aggregated into a single representation [LaTeX: \mathbf{v}_{\text{pool}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{model}}] 𝐯 pool ∈ ℝ d m ​ o ​ d ​ e ​ l \mathbf{v}_{\text{pool}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{model}} using a standard pooling function (e.g., Mean or Max pooling): (1) [LaTeX: \mathbf{v}_{\text{pool}}=\text{Pool}(V_{\text{keep}})] 𝐯 pool = Pool ​ ( V keep ) \mathbf{v}_{\text{pool}}=\text{Pool}(V_{\text{keep}}) This results in a standard dense embedding that fits into existing single-vector search indices. 3.3. Training Strategy To effectively train the filtering policy [LaTeX: \pi_{\theta}] π θ \pi_{\theta} without requiring annotated relevance labels, we propose a self-supervised training framework based on inverse retrieval . Unlike standard retrieval where a query is used to search for documents, our training objective inverts this relationship: the agent learns to pool a document such that the resulting vector provides high similarity to its corresponding synthetic queries. 3.3.1. Synthetic Query Generation We construct a training dataset by generating synthetic queries for each document in our corpus [LaTeX: \mathcal{D}] 𝒟 \mathcal{D} . For each document [LaTeX: d\in\mathcal{D}] d ∈ 𝒟 d\in\mathcal{D} , we utilize a Large Language Model (LLM) ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ) to generate a set of [LaTeX: k] k k distinct queries [LaTeX: \mathcal{Q}_{d}=\{q_{1},\dots,q_{k}\}] 𝒬 d = { q 1 , … , q k } \mathcal{Q}_{d}=\{q_{1},\dots,q_{k}\} relevant to [LaTeX: d] d d . This process yields a set of positive pairs [LaTeX: (d,q^{+})] ( d , q + ) (d,q^{+}) where [LaTeX: q^{+}\in\mathcal{Q}_{d}] q + ∈ 𝒬 d q^{+}\in\mathcal{Q}_{d} . 3.3.2. Pre-computation and Setup To enable efficient RL training, we treat the underlying embedding space as fixed. We pre-compute the multi-vector embeddings for all documents and the single-vector embeddings for all generated queries using the base embedding model [LaTeX: \mathcal{M}] ℳ \mathcal{M} : (2) [LaTeX: \displaystyle V_{d}] V d \displaystyle V_{d} [LaTeX: \displaystyle=\mathcal{M}(d)\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{model}}] = ℳ ⁡ ( d ) ∈ ℝ N × d m ​ o ​ d ​ e ​ l \displaystyle=\mathcal{M}(d)\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{model}} (3) [LaTeX: \displaystyle V_{q}] V q \displaystyle V_{q} [LaTeX: \displaystyle=\mathcal{M}(q)\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{model}}] = ℳ ⁡ ( q ) ∈ ℝ N × d m ​ o ​ d ​ e ​ l \displaystyle=\mathcal{M}(q)\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{model}} These pre-computed embeddings serve as the environment state for the RL agent. 3.3.3. Optimization via Inverse Retrieval Rank The training process iterates through the following steps to optimize the policy [LaTeX: \pi_{\theta}] π θ \pi_{\theta} : (1) Policy Rollout: Given a document embedding [LaTeX: V_{d}] V d V_{d} , the policy samples a mask [LaTeX: a\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|V_{d})] a ∼ π θ ( ⋅ | V d ) a\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|V_{d}) to select a subset of vectors [LaTeX: V_{\text{keep}}] V keep V_{\text{keep}} . (2) Pooling: The retained vectors are aggregated into a single document representation: (4) [LaTeX: \mathbf{v}_{\text{pool}}=\text{Pool}(V_{\text{keep}})] 𝐯 pool = Pool ​ ( V keep ) \mathbf{v}_{\text{pool}}=\text{Pool}(V_{\text{keep}}) (3) Inverse Retrieval Simulation: We treat [LaTeX: \mathbf{v}_{\text{pool}}] 𝐯 pool \mathbf{v}_{\text{pool}} as a query vector to search against the synthetic queries [LaTeX: \mathcal{Q}] 𝒬 \mathcal{Q} . The objective is to retrieve the ground-truth query [LaTeX: V_{q^{+}}] V q + V_{q^{+}} associated with document [LaTeX: d] d d from [LaTeX: \mathcal{Q}] 𝒬 \mathcal{Q} . Similarity scores are computed between [LaTeX: \mathbf{v}_{\text{pool}}] 𝐯 pool \mathbf{v}_{\text{pool}} and all queries in [LaTeX: \mathcal{Q}] 𝒬 \mathcal{Q} : (5) [LaTeX: s(d,\mathcal{Q})=\mathbf{v}_{\text{pool}}^{\top}\text{Pool}(V_{q})] s ⁡ ( d , 𝒬 ) = 𝐯 pool ⊤ ​ Pool ​ ( V q ) s(d,\mathcal{Q})=\mathbf{v}_{\text{pool}}^{\top}\text{Pool}(V_{q}) (4) Rank-Based Reward: We align the training objective with retrieval performance by using Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG) ( Järvelin and Kekäläinen, 2002 ) as the reward signal. NDCG is a standard information retrieval metric that evaluating ranking quality not only by the presence of relevant items, but also by their position in the list. For a given document [LaTeX: d] d d and its ground-truth query [LaTeX: q^{+}] q + q^{+} , we rank the set of synthetic queries [LaTeX: \mathcal{Q}] 𝒬 \mathcal{Q} based on their computed similarity scores. The reward is defined as: (6) [LaTeX: r=\text{NDCG}(q^{+},\mathcal{Q})] r = NDCG ​ ( q + , 𝒬 ) r=\text{NDCG}(q^{+},\mathcal{Q}) This formulation applies a logarithmic discount to the rank of the positive query, effectively penalizing the agent more for missing the top spots than for ordering errors deeper in the list. This encourages the model to prioritize features that are highly discriminative for the specific query. (5) Policy Update: The policy parameters are updated using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) ( Shao et al., 2024 ) to maximize the expected reward. GRPO estimates advantages by centering rewards within a group of samples, eliminating the need for a separate value network while maintaining stable policy updates similar to PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) . sections.title: 4. Experiments
sections.text: 4. Experiments We evaluate ReinPool on the Vidore V2 benchmark to answer three research questions: (1) What compression ratio does ReinPool achieve versus full multi-vector storage? (2) How much retrieval performance is preserved after compression? (3) Does learned pooling outperform static pooling baselines? 4.1. Experimental Setup Benchmark. We evaluate on Vidore V2 ( Faysse et al., 2024b ) , a comprehensive benchmark for visual document retrieval spanning four domains: ESG (Environmental, Social, Governance reports), ECO (Economic documents), ESGHL (ESG Highlights), and BIO (Biomedical literature). We report NDCG@3 for each subset and the average across all tasks. Embedding Models. We apply ReinPool to three state-of-the-art vision-language embedding models with varying architectures: • Tomoro-ColQwen-4b ( Huang and Tan, 2025 ) : 4B parameters, hidden dimension 320, average 1249 vectors per document. • NeMo-ColEmbed-3b ( NVIDIA, 2024 ) : 3B parameters, hidden dimension 3072, average 1802 vectors per document. • ColQwen2.5-3b ( Faysse, 2024 ) : 3B parameters, compact dimension 128, average 746 vectors per document. Baselines. We compare against: (1) Full Multi-Vector : the uncompressed representation storing all token embeddings; (2) Static Mean/Max Pooling : naive aggregation of all vectors into a single representation. Implementation Details. We implement ReinPool using the PyTorch framework. The filtering policy network is trained using the AdamW optimizer with a weight decay of [LaTeX: 0.01] 0.01 0.01 . We employ a learning rate scheduler ( ReduceLROnPlateau ) that halves the learning rate when the validation NDCG@3 score plateaus, ensuring fine-grained convergence. Gradients are clipped at a global norm of [LaTeX: 1.0] 1.0 1.0 to stabilize training. The RL training loop follows the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) ( Shao et al., 2024 ) paradigm. For every training step, inputs are repeated to generate a group of variations (determined by the group_size hyperparameter) by sampling masks from the policy. The reward signal is the NDCG@3 score computed against the ground-truth queries associated with the document. Advantages are estimated by centering the rewards within each group, effectively normalizing the signal without requiring a separate value network. The policy is updated to maximize the expected advantage-weighted log-likelihood of the selected actions. The base embedding models remain frozen throughout the training of the ReinPool policy to ensure computational efficiency. 4.2. Main Results Table 1 presents the retrieval results. We report Embedding Cost as the total dimensionality per document (Number of Vectors [LaTeX: \times] × \times Vector Dimension). Compression Efficiency. ReinPool achieves dramatic compression ratios across all models. For Tomoro-ColQwen-4b, storage is reduced from [LaTeX: 1249\times 320] 1249 × 320 1249\times 320 to [LaTeX: 1\times 320] 1 × 320 1\times 320 —a 1249 [LaTeX: \times] × \times reduction —while maintaining 76% of retrieval performance (37.65 vs. 49.48 NDCG@3). Similarly, ColQwen2.5-3b is compressed from [LaTeX: 746\times 128] 746 × 128 746\times 128 to [LaTeX: 1\times 128] 1 × 128 1\times 128 while recovering 81% of full performance (32.11 vs. 39.40). Superiority over Static Pooling. ReinPool consistently and substantially outperforms naive pooling. On Tomoro-ColQwen-4b, [LaTeX: \text{ReinPool}_{\text{Mean}}] ReinPool Mean \text{ReinPool}_{\text{Mean}} achieves 37.65 NDCG@3, a 22% absolute improvement over static mean pooling (30.76). For ColQwen2.5-3b, the improvement is even more pronounced: [LaTeX: \text{ReinPool}_{\text{Mean}}] ReinPool Mean \text{ReinPool}_{\text{Mean}} achieves 32.11 versus 24.16 for static mean ( +33% relative ). These gains demonstrate that the RL policy successfully identifies and preserves discriminative vectors that static methods dilute with non-informative content. Effect of Embedding Dimension. Compression effectiveness correlates with embedding dimensionality. For NeMo-ColEmbed-3b (dim 3072), both static pooling (8.66) and ReinPool (16.90) struggle to match full multi-vector performance (47.75), suggesting that extremely high-dimensional spaces contain fine-grained information difficult to compress into a single vector. However, ReinPool still achieves a 95% relative improvement over static mean pooling (16.90 vs. 8.66). Conversely, lower-dimensional models like ColQwen2.5-3b (dim 128) are highly amenable to learned pooling. Mean vs. Max Pooling. [LaTeX: \text{ReinPool}_{\text{Mean}}] ReinPool Mean \text{ReinPool}_{\text{Mean}} consistently outperforms [LaTeX: \text{ReinPool}_{\text{Max}}] ReinPool Max \text{ReinPool}_{\text{Max}} across all models, suggesting that mean aggregation better preserves the distributional properties learned by the embedding models. Nevertheless, [LaTeX: \text{ReinPool}_{\text{Max}}] ReinPool Max \text{ReinPool}_{\text{Max}} still provides substantial gains over static max pooling (e.g., 8.30 vs. 2.27 on Tomoro-ColQwen-4b).
